bleacher-busters: Started as a physics toy: how far can you hit a baseball before the numbers stop being funny. The history splits in two, gameplay and layout until the end of July, then release engineering, consent gates and age-rating calls after it.
wall-street-1987: The longest-running codebase here and the one with the messiest early history, because it started before there was any release process. The turn comes in July, when the project moved drives and every hardcoded path had to be repointed.
zero-day-syndicate: The most heavily tested thing in the portfolio: eight release candidates before anything reached a public track. One of them exists only because the game loop kept running while the phone was in a pocket.
water-polo-smash: A drag-back-and-shoot game whose entire difficulty curve lives in one number: how much of the ball has to be inside the frame to count as a goal. The rest of the work splits between presentation and the release grind.
marathon-kid: A training sim where the interesting problem is pacing rather than input: a season has to feel long enough to matter without becoming a chore. Store-prep stage, so the recent entries lean toward listing assets and release checks rather than mechanics.
stonewheel: A skateboarding game about lines and errands in equal measure. Built in a concentrated run from July onward, which is why the history is dense and the early scaffolding commits sit close to the gameplay ones.
bent-fc: By a wide margin the most-committed project here. A football management game where the corruption is the mechanic rather than a modifier, which means most of the log is balance work: what a bribe costs, what it buys, and how quickly the league notices.
cage-of-glory: A fighting-career sim built around one constraint, that a fight should be decided by preparation rather than by the button press. Long history, most of it spent on the ladder between club shows and a title shot.
domestique: A cycling career game about riding for someone else first. The log is mostly race simulation: how a breakaway forms, when a team gives up on a leader, and how to make a supporting role feel like a role rather than a penalty.
bikini-bay: A surf-camp builder where the board shaping and the business sim had to be made to care about each other. Most of the history is that integration rather than either half on its own.
chess-drill-instructor: A tactics trainer, deliberately narrow. The shortest log in the portfolio because the scope never moved: drill, feedback, repeat.
crystl-health: A supplement and health tracker built on the rule that nothing leaves the device. That constraint shaped the whole codebase, so the log has more storage and import/export work than feature work.
dork: A text adventure for a blind protagonist: no LOOK, only LISTEN, SMELL and FEEL. Most of the work is the parser and the long tail of edge cases that come with anything that has to understand what a player typed.
letterman: Letters, timers and a scoring rule that took several passes to stop rewarding the same safe play every round.
mise: A cookbook that does the tedious part: parse a recipe from a link, a PDF, a photo or pasted text, entirely on-device, then run the timers during the cook. Most of the log is parsing, because every recipe source on the internet is structured differently and none of them agree.
murder-phone: A text-message crime story where the interface is the constraint. Dense history because branching dialogue means every change touches more of the script than it looks like it should.
pubg-di: A drill trainer built to a fixed scope and left there. Seven entries, which is the honest length of a project that did what it needed to do early.
sauce-boss: A hot-sauce business sim. Short, recent history: the build is young and most of it is still the core loop.
young-homie: Early development. The log is scaffolding and prototype work rather than anything that resembles a finished loop yet.
california-trail: A trail-journey game in early development. Most entries are systems groundwork, the parts that have to exist before the travel loop can be tuned.
windward: An age-of-sail trading sim built around the idea that you should end up running a company rather than a boat. Early development, so the log is mostly the standing-orders system that the whole design depends on.
zero-cool: This project changed shape halfway through. Everything before 25 July 2026 is a solo hacking sim; after it the game is a street-to-kingpin crime empire, with hacking demoted to Chapter 1 and most of the engine carried over intact.
bent-fc-tournament: Started 9 August 2026 and immediately the densest commit rate here, because the sequel inherited a working match engine. Most of the work is the federation layer and its minigames: the envelope, the ballot, the shredder, the dossier.
rugpull: Young and moving fast: prologue, coin launch, weekly project loop and both endings are in. The art is deliberately not in the repository, it is generated locally from a licensed pack that cannot be redistributed.
office-politics: Nothing to a playable vertical slice: art pipeline, fight screen, and one complete fight with all thirteen powers. The honest next step is not more building, it is tuning a fight with one dominant power and a Heat meter that never bites.
rich-man-poor-man: A single static page with no backend, so almost every change is content or balance rather than plumbing. The scenario bank has grown well past the 370 it launched with.
crystl-suite: Built as internal tooling first and opened up afterwards. The decisive change removed the Express backend, so every tool now runs in the browser: static hosting, no server, no bill, no attack surface.
statclash: Short history, because these sites share almost everything through the monorepo's shared/ folder. What is committed here is the deck and the theme.
starclash: One commit, which is the honest length of a project carved out of another one. The GitHub deck used to live inside StatClash behind a deck picker, and two audiences with a menu in front of them is worse than two sites with none.
code-snob: The engine came free from shared/, so the work here was entirely content: 56 snippets sorted into 11 families. The families are the difficulty dial, not decoration.
font-guesser: Most of this project is not code, it is 54 font files and the licence check behind them. Self-hosting was the one decision that mattered: a specimen rendered in a fallback font is not a puzzle, it is a lie.
what-year: Sixty-five puzzles, each a film, a song and an event from one year, plus the daily plumbing that makes everyone see the same board.
inflation-price: The game is a text input and a slider's worth of logic. The work is the data: real launch prices and a CPI series from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, not a multiplier someone picked.
